newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks edge up on mixed earnings response.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks edge up on mixed earnings response.

text.p: Mexican stocks ended marginally ahead on Friday after zigzagging through the session as mixed reactions to first quarter earnings released through the day tussled with changing trends on Wall Street, traders said.
"Earnings were generally not very good, but the market took the blow as it had sagged a little earlier in the week and it also managed to fend off the slump in the Dow (Jones)," a desk trader said.
The leading IPC share index ended up 8.91 points, or 0.24 percent, at 3,782.62.
The Dow Jones, meanwhile, closed down 53.38 points at 6,738.87.
Another trader felt the bourse ended in positive territory after staging a last-minute recovery on buying fueled by brokers revaluating stocks for portfolio purposes.
"To be honest, I feel there was some window-dressing at the close," he said.
Dealers said the IPC mirrored erratic progress by market heavyweight Telmex, which ended flat at 16.44 pesos, while its ADRs closed off 1/4 at 41-1/2.
Traders' opinions were mixed on Telmex earnings, which were posted on Thursday evening.
"Operating earnings were up, the net was in line with forecasts, so the report was reasonable," one trader said.
Another trader said: "They bought ahead of something better, which is why it (Telmex) was off for most of the session."
Traders drew attention to a recovery by Mexico's two largest financial groups, Bancomer and Banacci, after both reporting positive earnings on Thursday evening.
"I think Bancomer and Banacci were oversold recently," a trader said.

Bancomer B shares ended up 18 centavos at 2.77 pesos to stand near the head of the prominent gainers' list and was the most traded stock of the session, accounting for 21 percent of all shares traded.
Banacci, meanwhile, rebounded 56 centavos to 16.98 pesos.
Media group Televisa was a prominent loser, off 2.50 pesos to 94.50 pesos on what traders said was a continuing reaction to poor earnings.
Trading volume was unremarkable at 81.1 million shares traded.

Some traders said the relative lack of dealing activity was due to open outcry being suspended on the trading floor for the day, following a fire in the Stock Exchange basement shortly after the close of trade on Thursday. All deals were settled by a screen trading system called SENTRA.
"I've been rushed off my feet, more than ever before," one desk trader said.
Said another: "Nothing happened, it was a dull day."
On the broad market, 107 stocks changed hands, of which gainers outnumbered decliners by 54 to 30.
(( --Martin Roberts, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-7907))
